review.sentence: Tyler and Harman differ completely on the tetrad's importance — Harman treats it as a major philosophical structure, Tyler calls the scientific claim preposterous — and they agree that it is not ordinary empirical science [3][4].

notes.quote: In this essay, the smartphone as a new technology and medium is analysed with regards to its effects on individuals and society. McLuhan’s tetrad serves as a framework for analysis, consisting of a set of four effects to examine media in their historical context and present environment as well as the characteristics and attributes of the medium itself.
notes.claim: A peer-reviewed student journal essay (Glocality, 2016) applies the tetrad as an analytic framework to the smartphone — an example of routine post-1988 applied tetrad work: enhancement (internet access, memory), obsolescence (feature phones, PCs, printers), retrieval (camera, e-books), reversal (augmented reality/Google Glass; communication that restricts interaction).

notes.quote: Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions. To sum up, it is a unique tool for “exploring the grammar of media”, as McLuhan put it
notes.claim: Even sympathetic appliers concede the tetrad is interpretive rather than predictive/verifiable: "multiple interpretations are possible", and its value is as a tool for "exploring the grammar of media" and for speculating about future developments.

notes.quote:
Published posthumously by his son Eric, _Laws of Media_ (1988) brought together McLuhan's ideas as a concise tetrad of media effects. These four laws of media further exhibit McLuhan's abiding concern with pedagogy: they are meant to be used as tools to analyze the patterns of effects that different technologies produce. McLuhan phrased them as questions with which to consider any artefact:

1. What does it enhance?
2. What does it make obsolete?
3. What does it retrieve that had been obsolesced earlier?
4. What does it flip into when pushed to extremes?
notes.claim: Library and Archives Canada gives the four laws in McLuhan's question form as published in Laws of Media (1988), posthumously edited by Eric McLuhan.

notes.quote: Considered as a _scientific_ _theory_, McLuhan's four "laws of media" risk violating communications research in a dangerously Procrustean manner. Conceived as an _exploratory probe_, however, this "tetrad" can provide illuminating insights into the social and psychological effects of individual technologies.
notes.claim: Tom Tyler's 2008 Game Studies article "A Procrustean Probe" frames the central critical verdict: taken as science the tetrad is Procrustean, but as a heuristic probe it has value — the double verdict the criticism section must convey.

notes.quote: This particular method is itself in danger of operating according to Procrustean principles: that is, bothersome empirical details which do not fit the theory are hammered or shorn in order that they be _made_ to fit.
notes.claim: Tyler's definition of the Procrustean charge: empirical details that do not fit are forcibly trimmed or stretched to fit the tetrad.

notes.quote: McLuhan asserted that they constituted testable hypotheses, and were a "scientific method" modelled on Popper's principle of falsifiability (1975, p. 75; 1977, p. 175). His son, Eric McLuhan, even suggests in _Laws of Media_, co-written with his father, that "they can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" (1988, p. 7).
notes.claim: Tyler records McLuhan's own claim that the tetrad was a falsifiable, Popperian scientific method — the claim critics then attack — and quotes Eric McLuhan's universality boast.

notes.quote: Applying the tetrad to the human artefact of _wine_, in order to discover its effects on individuals and society, they argue that it enhances "grape juice" (via fermentation), obsolesces "commonplace flavours", retrieves "ritual observance", and reverses into "cooking wine vinegar" (1988, p. 206). Or, at least, these are the answers the first time they apply the tetrad. In an alternative version on the same page, we find that wine enhances food and "the occasion", obsolesces "inhibition", retrieves "festive spontaneity of speech and gesture", and reverses into "hangover" and insult.
notes.claim: The two wine tetrads on p. 206 of Laws of Media, quoted exactly: first version enhances grape juice, obsolesces commonplace flavours, retrieves ritual observance, reverses into cooking wine vinegar; the alternative version enhances food and the occasion, obsolesces inhibition, retrieves festive spontaneity, reverses into hangover and insult.

notes.quote: Conceived as a universal "scientific method", the tetrad is far too vague: a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into. The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since illustrative examples can readily be stretched to fit.
notes.claim: Tyler's core unfalsifiability argument: as a universal scientific method the tetrad is too vague, any creative mind can fill the four slots for any artefact, so illustrative examples stretch to fit.

notes.quote: At the same time, just like Procrustes' bed, McLuhan's tetrad is unrelentingly rigid: it _requires_ us to fill the gaps. Do we really wish to suggest that wine obsolesces "commonplace flavours" or that it retrieves "ritual observance"? Perhaps, but we do violence to these complex notions when they are hewn to fit the tetrad's frame
notes.claim: The rigidity half of Tyler's double bind: the tetrad is unrelentingly rigid, requiring four slots to be filled, doing violence to complex notions hewn to fit its frame.

notes.quote: The idea that these are "scientific laws" in anything like the sense in which we ordinarily use that phrase is preposterous [\[7\]](#%5Fedn7). And yet the tetrad has its uses. In fact, it is best conceived, as McLuhan himself often did, as a heuristic device taking the form of a set of questions: _what_ does a technology enhance, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into (1977, p. 175)?
notes.claim: Tyler's blunt verdict on the scientific status claim, and his alternative: best conceived as a heuristic set of questions, a "probe" — quoting McLuhan's "I don't explain - I explore".

notes.quote: McLuhan was not simply claiming that one medium entirely supersedes another: clearly, newspapers did not die out with the advent of radio any more than "commonplace flavours" disappeared with the consumption of wine.
notes.claim: Tyler's point that McLuhan did not claim one medium wholly supersedes another — relevant to the determinism charge; the tetrad's obsolescence law is not simple replacement.

notes.quote: The idea behind the tetrad is that every human artifact does four separate things simultaneously: it enhances something, causes something else to become obsolete, retrieves an older medium that was previously dead, and eventually reverses into its opposite.
notes.claim: Harman's own summary of the tetrad's four operations, and his framing of the tetrad as a fourfold structure — the bridge between McLuhan and object-oriented metaphysics.

notes.quote: The division between the enhancement and obsolescence of any artifact is what the McLuhans call the “morphology” of an artifact. This morphology already incorporates, though in more practical and applicable form, the most important philosophical insight of the twentieth century: Martin Heidegger’s critique of presence-at-hand.
notes.claim: Harman's key extension: the tetrad's two axes are named morphology (enhancement/obsolescence) and metamorphosis (reversal/retrieval), and the morphology axis is read as a practical version of Heidegger's critique of presence-at-hand — the object exceeds its explicit content.

notes.quote: For a sustained critique, and McLuhan's response, see Venable (1976) and McLuhan (1976).
notes.claim: Tyler points readers to the Venable/McLuhan 1976 exchange as the sustained critique of the tetrad — the standard scholarly citation for early criticism.

notes.quote: The laws are modelled in part after Bacon's four idols and Vico's four axioms; see McLuhan and McLuhan (1988, pp. 3-11 \[Introduction\]).
notes.claim: Tyler's account of the tetrad's derivation: modelled in part on Bacon's four idols and Vico's four axioms — supports the criticism that the fourfold frame is imposed a priori rather than derived from evidence.

notes.quote: Yet perhaps the more important part of the tetrad is the axis between reversal and retrieval, which the McLuhans call “metamorphosis.” That is to say, unlike Heidegger, they pay a good deal of attention to cases in which the hidden and the visible change roles at various points in history.
notes.claim: Harman's second axis: reversal/retrieval is "metamorphosis"; unlike Heidegger, the McLuhans attend to historical role-reversals between hidden and visible — the basis of Harman's claim that the tetrad is more than a Heideggerian fourfold.

notes.quote: In a word, retrieval requires _decontextualization_. Second, the content of the old medium cannot be straightforwardly retrieved since it will need to be adapted to new circumstances.
notes.claim: Harman's own extension of retrieval into design theory: retrieval is the quadrant under human control and requires decontextualization plus adaptation, i.e. translation — his example is Tschumi's Le Fresnoy. This is how the tetrad is extended into architecture/design rather than left as media analysis.

notes.quote: The danger with any theory or schema is that it inevitably does violence to its subject matter. Such violence is redeemed only if the resulting investigation is ultimately constructive.
notes.claim: Tyler's concession that any schema does violence to its subject matter — the critical verdict in his own words, useful for framing the criticism as constructive rather than dismissive.

notes.quote:
The laws are based on a set of four questions - a tetrad - that can be applied to any artefact or idea:
What does it enhance or intensify?
What does it render obsolete or displace?
What does it retrieve that was previoulsy obsolesced?
What does it produce or become when pressed to an extreme?
 Inherent in every human innovation is an answer to each of the questions of this tetrad; anything that does not contain answers to these four questions is not the product of human creation.
The laws identified by the McLuhans consitute a new scientific basis for media studies, testable, and able to allow for prediction.
notes.claim: The publisher's own description of Laws of Media: The New Science gives the tetrad's four questions and explicitly claims scientific, testable, predictive status for the laws, plus a definitional completeness claim.

notes.quote: McLuhan asserted that they constituted testable hypotheses, and were a "scientific method" modelled on Popper's principle of falsifiability (1975, p. 75; 1977, p. 175). His son, Eric McLuhan, even suggests in _Laws of Media_, co-written with his father, that "they can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" (1988, p. 7). This is not, in fact, the case, as one of the McLuhans' own examples illustrates.
notes.claim: The tetrad was offered as Popperian testable hypotheses, checkable by anyone anywhere; Tyler says this is not the case, using the McLuhans' own wine example. Establishes what would count as a test (repeatable, checkable answers) and that the claim fails it.

notes.quote: Conceived as a universal "scientific method", the tetrad is far too vague: a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into. The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since illustrative examples can readily be stretched to fit.
notes.claim: Core criticism bearing on testability: the tetrad is too vague to falsify because any artefact's four answers can be stretched to fit. This is the central obstacle to any empirical test.

notes.quote: At the same time, just like Procrustes' bed, McLuhan's tetrad is unrelentingly rigid: it _requires_ us to fill the gaps.
notes.claim: The second half of the double bind: the tetrad is also rigid, forcing four filled quadrants whether or not evidence exists — the opposite failure to vagueness, and a design flaw for any coding scheme.

notes.quote: but it is clear that existing studies are collectively uncertain on the question of whether the enhancement of digital play is at the same time obsolescing television
notes.claim: The closest thing to an empirical check in the literature: Tyler tested the obsolescence quadrant for digital games against Dutch, cross-European, Kaiser Family Foundation and Nick Yee data, and found the studies collectively uncertain (Kaiser found no displacement; Yee's MMORPG data suggested displacement). Shows what a partial test looks like and that results are equivocal.

notes.quote: Perhaps the overambitiously phrased and deterministic laws of media can contribute to the creation of distinctions between different kinds of effects; if so, it can be worthwhile to try them out.
notes.claim: An anthropologist's explicit trial of the tetrad on the Internet, 1996: he judges the laws "overambitiously phrased and deterministic" but worth trying out to distinguish kinds of effects. This is the clearest case of a scholar putting the tetrad to a use-test rather than a formal experiment.

notes.quote: The Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics.
notes.claim: Eriksen's own trial collapses: all four laws return the same answer for the Internet and identity politics — a concrete demonstration, from an attempt to use it, that the tetrad cannot discriminate outcomes, which is the practical face of unfalsifiability.

notes.quote: Additionally, the tetrad allows one to reflect the past and to try to predict – or at least speculate – about future developments.
notes.claim: The Glocality essay concedes that its four quadrants are interpretive, and that the tetrad only licenses speculation about reversal rather than verification; it also supports claims with outside empirical studies rather than testing the tetrad itself — showing the pattern where the tetrad frames but does not generate testable predictions.

notes.quote: Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions.
notes.claim: The Glocality smartphone tetrad is typical of post-1988 applications: it is an interpretive essay, not a test — the author concedes that multiple interpretations are possible, which is exactly what a falsifiable procedure could not allow.

notes.quote: Surveying a range of games and platforms from _Pong_ (Atari, 1972) and _Pac-Man_ (Namco, 1980) to _Myst_ (Cyan Worlds, 1993) and _Virtual Valerie_ (Reactor, 1990), they argue that computer games provide multiple examples of such remediation
notes.claim: Tyler's method is the closest available model of a test: each quadrant must engage existing empirical research (Kaiser Family Foundation media-use surveys, Nick Yee's MMORPG data), and where the evidence cuts against the quadrant he reports it and redefines the term (obsolescence as remediation). This is a test of the tetrad's fit against data, not of the tetrad's predictions.

notes.quote: This paper summarizes how the McLuhan Tetrad help the students to handle the laser cleaning technique as a case of study.
notes.claim: The tetrad travelled outside media studies into engineering and innovation management: a 2018 Springer conference paper (Engineering Digital Transformation, Lecture Notes in Management and Industrial Engineering, pp. 265–273) uses the McLuhan tetrad in a Project Management course to analyse laser cleaning machines as a technological innovation.

notes.quote: When faced with a requirement to evaluate, a feature to test, a test approach, or an organizational change, the Laws of Media might help you notice what might be extended, retrieved, and obsolesced
notes.claim: Design/professional practice application: software tester Michael Bolton's "McLuhan for Testers" (Better Software, October 2007) repurposes the tetrad as a set of "probes"/heuristics for evaluating new requirements, features and organizational changes — e.g. treating a dedicated test team as a medium with enhancement, retrieval, obsolescence and reversal effects.

notes.quote:
# The Tetrad and Phenomenology
* **By** Graham Harman
* **Source:** Explorations in Media Ecology, Volume 6, Issue 3, Sep 2007, p. 189 - 196
notes.claim: Bibliographic record of Harman's dedicated tetrad article: "The Tetrad and Phenomenology," Explorations in Media Ecology 6(3), Sept 2007, pp. 189–196 — evidence that Harman carried the tetrad into a full phenomenological argument in the media-ecology journal, not just a passing remark.

notes.quote: In his later career, McLuhan worked with his son Eric to reorganize his thought into a fourfold structure known as the “tetrad.”
notes.claim: Harman places the tetrad in a longer McLuhan lineage: it was a late-career fourfold worked out with Eric McLuhan, and its morphology axis is credited with containing Heidegger's critique of presence-at-hand "in more practical and applicable form" — the core of the object-oriented reading.

notes.quote: the researchers found both that the total time spent using media had not changed (2005, p. 37), and that increasing use of 'new' media such digital games did not displace 'old' media such as television.
notes.claim: Empirical evidence gathered by Tyler against the obsolescence quadrant: the Kaiser Family Foundation's studies of 8–18 year-olds found total media time unchanged and no displacement of old media by new — the predicted effect simply did not appear.

notes.quote: "MMORPG gamers spend on average 21.0 hours per week playing the game … and spend on average 7.7 hours per week watching TV … The national average for TV watching per week is around 28, which is what the above averages add up to. In other words, this lends support to the claim that time that was spent watching TV has been displaced by MMORPG playing" (Yee, 2005).
notes.claim: Counter-evidence Tyler sets against the Kaiser finding: Nick Yee's Daedalus Project MMORPG survey (21.0 hrs/week gaming, 7.7 hrs/week TV, adding up to the ~28-hour national TV average) supports displacement — so the one quadrant subjected to real data yields contradictory results.

notes.quote: Accurate and detailing records of the time individuals spend with a particular medium is frequently hard to obtain, and virtually impossible after the event
notes.claim: Why even a partial test is hard: Tyler lists the practical obstacles to verifying the obsolescence law — poor time-use records, multitasking and convergence, and the difficulty of establishing causal displacement between media.

notes.quote: The diversity of results from the tetrad's application need not be a problem--once we dispense with pretensions to scientific uniformity--so long as these provide illuminating insights into the matter at hand.
notes.claim: The most defensible verdict in the literature: the tetrad's variable results stop being a problem only if the claim to scientific uniformity is abandoned — so what can be "tested" is its heuristic fruitfulness, not its laws. This is the resolution most writers adopt.

notes.quote: The idea that these are "scientific laws" in anything like the sense in which we ordinarily use that phrase is preposterous
notes.claim: Tyler explicitly ranks the tetrad as a heuristic, not a science — "the idea that these are 'scientific laws' … is preposterous" — while still using it. That verdict frames the empirical question: nothing in the literature treats it as a testable law, only as a probe whose usefulness is judged case by case.

notes.quote: It is important to remember that these four laws exist simultaneously. Although McLuhan sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order. The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool, but one for exploration of the "grammar and syntax" of each artefact, a dynamic tool to describe "situations that are in process."
notes.claim: The four laws operate simultaneously, not sequentially, and McLuhan's own centre of interest was the 'grammar and syntax' of artefacts rather than scientific prediction; LAC notes he sometimes spoke as if they succeeded each other.

notes.quote: The McLuhans are retrieving another way of understanding our world, a way known to some ancient Greeks (but not Aristotle), to medieval thinkers, to Francis Bacon and Giambattista Vico, and to T.S. Eliot and James Joyce in this century. It is based on the use of words and the conseuqent power of the 'logos' to shape all the elements of culture - media - with which we surround ourselves.
notes.claim: The publisher presents the tetrad's lineage as a recovery of an older, pre-Aristotelian/logos-based way of understanding (ancient Greeks 'but not Aristotle', medieval thinkers, Bacon, Vico, Eliot, Joyce) and states the scope as all human artefacts, with a completeness claim that makes the tetrad definitional.

notes.quote: 'Media,' the word so closely connected with Marshall McLuhan's thought, is here explored in its broadest meaning, encompassing all that has been created by humans: artefacts, information, ideas - every example of human innovation, from computer program to a tea cup, from musical arrangement to the formula for a cold remedy, from an X-ray machine to the sentence you're reading right now. All these are media to whcih can be applied the laws the McLuhans have developed.
notes.claim: The book's scope claim: 'media' means everything humans make, and the four questions are held to have an answer inherent in every human innovation — so an artefact without tetrad answers is, by definition, not a human product.

notes.quote: Applying the tetrad to the human artefact of _wine_, in order to discover its effects on individuals and society, they argue that it enhances "grape juice" (via fermentation), obsolesces "commonplace flavours", retrieves "ritual observance", and reverses into "cooking wine vinegar" (1988, p. 206).
notes.claim: Reproducibility failure, the minimal requirement for any test: on a single page of Laws of Media the McLuhans give two incompatible tetrads for wine, so independent applications do not converge even when the same authors apply the same instrument.

notes.quote: They can be **asked (and the answers checked**) by anyone, anywhere, at any…
notes.claim: Verbatim snippet from Laws of Media itself (via Open Library full-text search of the 1988 edition): the McLuhans claim the four questions 'can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any' time — the book's own universal-checkability claim, the status claim critics later attacked.

notes.quote: they can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact
notes.claim: What the McLuhans themselves claimed for the tetrad sets the bar any test would have to meet: Eric McLuhan's assertion that the four questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" — a claim of universal, repeatable checkability that Tyler says the wine example refutes.

notes.quote: My one objection to how the McLuhans present this morphological pair is that they sometimes speak as if “enhance” meant “to make more visible,” though by their own principles, it should actually mean “to make into more of a hidden medium while downplaying visible content.”
notes.claim: Harman's internal criticism of the tetrad's own vocabulary: the McLuhans use "enhance" as if it meant making something more visible, when their principles imply enhancement makes a medium more hidden.

notes.quote: Reversal is the easier of the two to explain, and for the McLuhans, it is largely outside our control.
notes.claim: Harman distinguishes reversal (outside human control) from retrieval (under direct human control) — the basis for treating retrieval as the design-relevant quadrant.

notes.quote: The majority rejection of McLuhan’s canonical status is usually based on one of two reasons: (1) he was a flashy media pundit rather than a serious academic figure, or (2) he was a technological determinist exposed as shallow by the Leftist authority Raymond Williams.
notes.claim: Harman lists the two standard grounds for rejecting McLuhan's canonical status, the second being the charge of technological determinism pressed by Raymond Williams — the determinism criticism the tetrad section must address.

notes.quote: The other metamorphic form of the McLuhans, retrieval, is under more direct human control, and is therefore perhaps of greater interest.
notes.claim: Harman states that retrieval — one of the tetrad's four quadrants — is under direct human control, and he later makes it the design-relevant quadrant (decontextualization plus adaptation). So a source read for this section does show a tetrad analysis in which users' choices determine the outcome, contrary to the section's claim that none does; Harman also says reversal is "largely outside our control."

notes.quote: Both decontextualization and adaptation are forms of _translation_, and this is precisely what the artist or designer is: a translator able to avoid a literal repeating of old forms.
notes.claim: Harman's design extension: decontextualization and adaptation are both forms of translation, and the designer is the translator who avoids literal repetition of old forms.

notes.quote: Surveying a range of games and platforms from _Pong_ (Atari, 1972) and _Pac-Man_ (Namco, 1980) to _Myst_ (Cyan Worlds, 1993) and _Virtual Valerie_ (Reactor, 1990), they argue that computer games provide multiple examples of such remediation
notes.claim: Tyler's strongest counter to the determinism charge: where displacement cannot be shown, he redefines obsolescence as remediation, citing Bolter and Grusin's finding that computer games remediate earlier media rather than replace them.

report.body:
## TL;DR

*Laws of Media* (1988) claims four questions hold for any human artefact — what it enhances, obsolesces, retrieves, and reverses into when pushed to extremes — and its publisher calls them "a new scientific basis for media studies, testable, and able to allow for prediction" [5]. Scholars have used the tetrad almost entirely as a heuristic: applied to smartphones, laser-cleaning machines and software testing, extended by Graham Harman into a Heideggerian fourfold, and defended by Tom Tyler as a "probe" while he calls the scientific claim "preposterous" [3]. No one has tested it as a set of laws. The McLuhans give two incompatible tetrads for wine on one page [3], and the one quadrant anyone has checked against survey data — obsolescence — comes out contradictory [3]. The empirical verdict is likely negative; the heuristic verdict is still open.

## Key Findings

- The four laws are questions, not statements, and they are claimed to be exhaustive by definition: "anything that does not contain answers to these four questions is not the product of human creation" [5].
- The book's publisher claims scientific, testable, predictive status for the laws [5], while Library and Archives Canada's own gloss says "The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool" [2]. The status dispute is internal to the McLuhan material.
- The fourfold is inherited from Bacon's idols and Vico's axioms rather than derived from evidence about media [3][5].
- Post-1988 use is overwhelmingly applied and single-artefact: a smartphone tetrad conceding that "multiple interpretations are possible" [1], a project-management course using the tetrad on laser cleaning [7], and a software-testing heuristic [8]. None reports independent coders, a coding scheme or a check against data.
- Graham Harman's is the substantial philosophical extension: enhancement/obsolescence is the "morphology" axis, reversal/retrieval the "metamorphosis" axis, and retrieval is the quadrant under human control, requiring decontextualization and adaptation — the basis of a design principle [4][9].
- Tyler's double bind is the central criticism: the tetrad is too vague to falsify, because "a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things" [3], and too rigid, because it "requires us to fill the gaps" [3].
- Reproducibility fails at the first hurdle. On p. 206 of *Laws of Media* wine both enhances "grape juice" and obsolesces "commonplace flavours", and in a second version on the same page enhances food and obsolesces "inhibition" [3].
- Eriksen's 1996 trial on the Internet produced the same answer in all four quadrants — "intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics" — a demonstration that the procedure cannot discriminate outcomes [6].
- The only quadrant-level empirical check, Tyler's on obsolescence for digital games, finds the evidence contradictory: Kaiser Family Foundation surveys found no displacement, Nick Yee's MMORPG data suggested displacement, and Tyler concludes the studies are "collectively uncertain" [3].
- No study located treats the four laws as hypotheses to be confirmed or refuted; the applied literature makes interpretive, pedagogical and practical claims instead [1][7][8].

## Details

### 1. What Laws of Media (1988) actually claimed: the four laws, their exact wording, their derivation, and the status claimed for them

*Laws of Media: The New Science* was published by the University of Toronto Press in 1988, eight years after McLuhan's death, completed and edited by his son Eric. Library and Archives Canada's guide to the McLuhan papers says the book "brought together McLuhan's ideas as a concise tetrad of media effects" [2].

The laws are four questions asked of any artefact, not four statements. In the publisher's formulation: "What does it enhance or intensify? What does it render obsolete or displace? What does it retrieve that was previoulsy obsolesced? What does it produce or become when pressed to an extreme?" [5]. Library and Archives Canada gives the same set with the fourth law as "What does it flip into when pushed to extremes?", and adds that the laws "are meant to be used as tools to analyze the patterns of effects that different technologies produce" [2].

The scope is deliberately total. "Media" is "here explored in its broadest meaning, encompassing all that has been created by humans: artefacts, information, ideas" [5]. The tetrad is then claimed to be exhaustive by definition: "Inherent in every human innovation is an answer to each of the questions of this tetrad; anything that does not contain answers to these four questions is not the product of human creation" [5]. That sentence is a claim about what counts as a human artefact, not a generalisation from cases. The distinction matters for the testability question in section 5.

On status, the book's own apparatus claims science. The publisher states that "The laws identified by the McLuhans consitute a new scientific basis for media studies, testable, and able to allow for prediction" [5]. Eric McLuhan, in the book, is quoted as saying the questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" (1988, p. 7) [3]. McLuhan had already presented the four laws in 1975 as testable hypotheses. Tyler records that they were offered as a "scientific method" modelled on Popper's principle of falsifiability [3].

Two features of the claim are easy to miss. First, the laws are simultaneous, not sequential: "It is important to remember that these four laws exist simultaneously" [2]. Second, the McLuhan apparatus does not agree with itself about the tetrad's status. Library and Archives Canada's gloss says "The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool, but one for exploration of the "grammar and syntax" of each artefact, a dynamic tool to describe "situations that are in process."" [2]. The scientific claim and the heuristic claim therefore sit in the same body of material, in the publisher's copy and in the archive's description. The dispute about status is internal before it is external.

The fourfold frame is inherited rather than derived. Tyler notes that the laws are "modelled in part after Bacon's four idols and Vico's four axioms" [3]. The publisher places the tetrad in a lineage running through "some ancient Greeks (but not Aristotle), to medieval thinkers, to Francis Bacon and Giambattista Vico, and to T.S. Eliot and James Joyce", resting on "the conseuqent power of the 'logos' to shape all the elements of culture" [5]. Neither account derives the four slots from evidence about media. The number four arrives first, and the questions are fitted to it. That is an inference from the two sources, and it is the hinge on which much of the criticism in section 4 turns.

What the laws do not claim matters, because the criticism often assumes otherwise. Obsolescence is not extinction. Tyler notes that "newspapers did not die out with the advent of radio any more than "commonplace flavours" disappeared with the consumption of wine" [3]. Reversal is the fourth question, not a forecast of progress.

### 2. How scholars have applied the tetrad since 1988: media ecology, Levinson's tetrad wheels, Logan's new media, design and digital-media work

The post-1988 literature is overwhelmingly applied rather than theoretical. The characteristic form is a single artefact, a single author, four quadrants and a conclusion that the artefact is more double-edged than it looks. Three examples located and read in this pass show the range of venues.

The first is a student-written, peer-reviewed essay in *Glocality* (2016) that runs the tetrad on the smartphone. It states its method plainly: "the smartphone as a new technology and medium is analysed with regards to its effects on individuals and society" [1]. The tetrad is the framework, and its four effects are used to place the device in its historical context and in its present environment [1]. The quadrants are filled in the expected way: internet access and memory enhanced, feature phones and printers obsolesced, the camera and the e-book retrieved, augmented reality and interaction-blocking communication as the reversal. The essay's own summary of its value is modest, calling the tetrad a tool for exploring the grammar of media, McLuhan's own phrase [1].

The second shows the frame travelling into engineering education. A conference paper titled "Lessons for Technological Innovation Analysis. A Case of Study Based on McLuhan Tetrad Applied to Laser Cleaning Machines" states: "This paper summarizes how the McLuhan Tetrad help the students to handle the laser cleaning technique as a case of study" [7]. The tetrad here is a teaching device for getting students to think about an unfamiliar technology's secondary effects, and the claim made for it is pedagogical. The paper's own text was not obtained in full, so the description rests on its title and abstract.

The third shows it travelling into professional practice. Software tester Michael Bolton's "McLuhan for Testers" (*Better Software*, October 2007) turns the tetrad into a checklist for requirements and organisational change: "When faced with a requirement to evaluate, a feature to test, a test approach, or an organizational change, the Laws of Media might help you notice what might be extended, retrieved, and obsolesced" [8]. The move is explicit — the four laws become "probes", a set of questions to ask before signing off on a change, including of a dedicated test team treated as a medium in its own right [8].

What these three share is a method and a limit. None reports independent coders, a coding scheme, a comparison against a rival analysis or a check of the quadrants against data. The Glocality essay is candid that the results are author-dependent: "Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions" [1]. Its predictive claim is similarly hedged: the tetrad "allows one to reflect the past and to try to predict – or at least speculate – about future developments" [1].

That pattern is the finding, not a complaint about individual papers. The frame has been applied to a smartphone, a laser-cleaning machine and a test team. It has demonstrated portability across a student journal, an engineering conference and a software-testing magazine. It has not demonstrated that its answers are the right ones, and the applied literature reviewed here does not attempt to. The one place where the tetrad has been pushed toward a discipline with criteria is Graham Harman's use of retrieval as a principle for design, which is treated in section 3 [4].

Two limits on this section should be stated. The selection above is what could be read in full within this pass, not a census; searches also surfaced applied tetrad papers on video conferencing, Microsoft Teams, cop-watching and soundscape composition, but only their bibliographic records were obtained and they are not cited here. And the venue distribution — a student journal, a conference proceedings, a trade magazine — is itself evidence about where this kind of work is published, not about how much of it exists.

### 3. How the tetrad has been extended: object-oriented metaphysics (Harman), fourfold logic, algorithmic and AI media, formal and computational versions

The most substantial philosophical extension of the tetrad came from outside media studies. Graham Harman, a philosopher of object-oriented ontology, treats the four laws as a fourfold of the same kind he looks for in any philosophy. His summary of the claim is exact: "every human artifact does four separate things simultaneously: it enhances something, causes something else to become obsolete, retrieves an older medium that was previously dead, and eventually reverses into its opposite" [4]. He dates the tetrad to McLuhan's late career, when "McLuhan worked with his son Eric to reorganize his thought into a fourfold structure known as the “tetrad.”" [4].

Harman's extension is to name the two axes and give each a philosophical job. "The division between the enhancement and obsolescence of any artifact is what the McLuhans call the “morphology” of an artifact", and this morphology "already incorporates, though in more practical and applicable form, the most important philosophical insight of the twentieth century: Martin Heidegger’s critique of presence-at-hand" [4]. The point is that an object is never exhausted by its explicit content; it carries background effects. The second axis is the more important one for Harman: "perhaps the more important part of the tetrad is the axis between reversal and retrieval, which the McLuhans call “metamorphosis.”" That axis is where "the hidden and the visible change roles at various points in history" [4]. This is what he holds distinguishes the tetrad from a Heideggerian fourfold, and he developed it at length in a dedicated article, "The Tetrad and Phenomenology," in *Explorations in Media Ecology* 6(3), 2007 [9].

Two consequences follow for anyone using the tetrad. The first is a distinction in agency: "Reversal is the easier of the two to explain, and for the McLuhans, it is largely outside our control" [4]. Retrieval, by contrast, is the quadrant where human work actually happens, which is why Harman turns it into a principle for architecture and design. Using Bernard Tschumi's Le Fresnoy art centre as his case, he argues retrieval has two conditions. The first is decontextualization, because the original functional context cannot be restored. The second is that the old medium's content "cannot be straightforwardly retrieved since it will need to be adapted to new circumstances" [4]. Both are forms of translation, and the designer is "a translator able to avoid a literal repeating of old forms" [4].

The second consequence is an internal criticism that bears directly on how the quadrants should be read. Harman objects that "they sometimes speak as if “enhance” meant “to make more visible,” though by their own principles, it should actually mean “to make into more of a hidden medium while downplaying visible content.”" [4]. If that is right, the enhancement quadrant is systematically misdescribed in the McLuhans' own usage — an inference from their figure/ground premises rather than a finding about media, but one that changes what a tetrad analyst should be looking for.

The extension also has a cost. Harman's reading makes the tetrad a universal structure of objects rather than a tool specific to media. That widens its scope and weakens its empirical content at the same time, since a fourfold true of every object cannot discriminate between objects. He also imposes a condition on any fourfold, including this one: it should be generated by crossing two prior distinctions deep enough to bear the weight, not assembled from whatever four terms are handy [4]. On that test the tetrad's warrant depends on figure/ground and on metamorphosis being real distinctions, not on the four labels themselves.

Beyond Harman, the extensions this pass could verify are thinner than the question assumes. Searches located later work that applies the tetrad to new media objects — a tetrad for video conferencing, one for Microsoft Teams in pandemic teaching, tetrads for generative AI and intellectual property — but only bibliographic records were obtained for these, not the texts, so no claim is made here about what they argue. Harman's own use of the tetrad to organise a philosophy of objects is the clearest documented case of the laws being extended into a formal structure rather than applied to one more device.

### 4. Criticism: from Venable (1976) and the Technology and Culture exchange to Tyler's Procrustean probe — unfalsifiability, rigidity, determinism, and the McLuhans' own two tetrads for wine

The criticism began before the book did. McLuhan published the four laws in *Technology and Culture* in 1975, and the exchange that followed is still the standard citation for the early critique: Tyler points readers to "Venable (1976) and McLuhan (1976)" as "a sustained critique, and McLuhan's response" [3]. The two 1976 items are indexed as "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" and "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws" [3]. Their texts were not obtained in this pass, so the summary of Venable's argument here rests on Tyler's use of it rather than on the letters themselves.

The most fully developed critique found in this pass is Tom Tyler's "A Procrustean Probe" (*Game Studies*, 2008). Its verdict is double, and the doubling is the argument. "Considered as a _scientific_ _theory_, McLuhan's four "laws of media" risk violating communications research in a dangerously Procrustean manner. Conceived as an _exploratory probe_, however, this "tetrad" can provide illuminating insights into the social and psychological effects of individual technologies" [3]. The frame fails as science and works as a prompt. The name is taken from the bandit who stretched or cut his guests to fit his bed: "This particular method is itself in danger of operating according to Procrustean principles: that is, bothersome empirical details which do not fit the theory are hammered or shorn in order that they be _made_ to fit" [3].

Tyler's two objections pull in opposite directions at once, and this is what makes the critique more than the usual charge of vagueness. First, the tetrad is too loose. "Conceived as a universal "scientific method", the tetrad is far too vague: a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into. The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since illustrative examples can readily be stretched to fit" [3]. Second, it is too tight. "At the same time, just like Procrustes' bed, McLuhan's tetrad is unrelentingly rigid: it _requires_ us to fill the gaps. Do we really wish to suggest that wine obsolesces "commonplace flavours" or that it retrieves "ritual observance"? Perhaps, but we do violence to these complex notions when they are hewn to fit the tetrad's frame" [3]. A frame that can absorb any answer and yet insists on four answers is a template, not a hypothesis. That is an inference from Tyler's two sentences. It also explains why the vagueness charge and the rigidity charge are compatible rather than contradictory.

The decisive evidence is the McLuhans' own wine tetrad, which appears twice on a single page. "Applying the tetrad to the human artefact of _wine_, in order to discover its effects on individuals and society, they argue that it enhances "grape juice" (via fermentation), obsolesces "commonplace flavours", retrieves "ritual observance", and reverses into "cooking wine vinegar" (1988, p. 206). Or, at least, these are the answers the first time they apply the tetrad. In an alternative version on the same page, we find that wine enhances food and "the occasion", obsolesces "inhibition", retrieves "festive spontaneity of speech and gesture", and reverses into "hangover" and insult" [3]. Two incompatible tetrads, same authors, same artefact, same page. The McLuhans claim the questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" [3]. If that were so, the answers should not diverge on one page.

On the status claim Tyler is blunt: "The idea that these are "scientific laws" in anything like the sense in which we ordinarily use that phrase is preposterous" [3]. His constructive alternative is the one most later writers adopt: treat the tetrad "as a heuristic device taking the form of a set of questions", which is what McLuhan himself often did [3]. He concedes the frame's real virtue — it directs attention to an artefact's operation rather than to its content — and he concedes the general point that "The danger with any theory or schema is that it inevitably does violence to its subject matter. Such violence is redeemed only if the resulting investigation is ultimately constructive" [3].

The determinism charge is older and broader, and it attaches to McLuhan's work as a whole more than to the tetrad. Harman, writing to defend McLuhan, summarises the standard grounds for rejecting him: he was dismissed either as "a flashy media pundit rather than a serious academic figure" or as "a technological determinist exposed as shallow by the Leftist authority Raymond Williams" [4]. The tetrad's structure cuts against the simplest version of the charge. Reversal and retrieval both describe media acting on each other, not a technology driving history one way. Tyler's point that obsolescence is not extinction supports that reading [3]. The charge is not fully answered, though. The tetrad still assigns the initiative to the artefact. Harman's reading does give one quadrant to human agency, since retrieval "is under more direct human control" while reversal is "largely outside our control" [4]. That concession covers a designer's use of old media, not the general direction of a medium's effects.

Tyler's substantive defence is different and stronger. Where displacement cannot be shown, he does not force the obsolescence quadrant. He reports that the studies are uncertain and then redefines obsolescence as remediation, drawing on Bolter and Grusin: "Surveying a range of games and platforms from _Pong_ (Atari, 1972) and _Pac-Man_ (Namco, 1980) to _Myst_ (Cyan Worlds, 1993) and _Virtual Valerie_ (Reactor, 1990), they argue that computer games provide multiple examples of such remediation" [3]. On that reading a new medium refashions its predecessors rather than extinguishing them, and the charge of one-way technological determinism loses its target.

A third line of criticism is internal and comes from a sympathiser. Harman objects that the McLuhans "sometimes speak as if “enhance” meant “to make more visible,” though by their own principles, it should actually mean “to make into more of a hidden medium while downplaying visible content.”" [4]. If enhancement is really a hiding, then the quadrant that looks most concrete in ordinary use is the one most likely to be filled in backwards. The critics do not converge on a common verdict. Tyler calls the scientific claim preposterous and keeps the tetrad as a heuristic [3]. Harman treats it as a major philosophical structure and does not address its scientific status at all [4]. The live dispute is therefore not whether the tetrad is falsifiable. It is whether a generative instrument that cannot be falsified is worth having, and if so under what discipline.

### 5. Has anyone tested it empirically? What has been attempted, what counts as a test, and what the results show

The bar for a test is set by the McLuhans, not by their critics. Eric McLuhan's claim that the four questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" [3] is a claim of universal, repeatable checkability. A test of that claim needs only two things: two competent analysts applying the questions to the same artefact, and a comparison of their answers.

The first attempt fails at that minimum. As section 4 sets out, the McLuhans produce two incompatible tetrads for wine on a single page of *Laws of Media* [3]. Two applications by the same two authors to the same artefact do not converge, so independent applications by anyone else have no reason to.

The clearest deliberate trial found is a 1996 paper posted on a University of Oslo personal page. Its author states the purpose plainly: "Perhaps the overambitiously phrased and deterministic laws of media can contribute to the creation of distinctions between different kinds of effects; if so, it can be worthwhile to try them out" [6]. That is a use-test, not an experiment, and the result is the most damaging single datum in this report. Applied to the Internet and identity politics, all four quadrants return the same answer: "The Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics" [6]. A procedure whose four outputs collapse into one cannot discriminate between outcomes, which is the practical face of unfalsifiability.

The nearest thing to an empirical check of a single quadrant is Tyler's treatment of obsolescence for digital games. He does not test the tetrad as a whole. He takes the quadrant's implied prediction — that a new medium displaces an old one — and sets existing survey data against it. The Kaiser Family Foundation's studies of 8- to 18-year-olds found "both that the total time spent using media had not changed (2005, p. 37), and that increasing use of 'new' media such digital games did not displace 'old' media such as television" [3]. Against that, Tyler quotes Nick Yee's Daedalus Project survey of MMORPG players: "MMORPG gamers spend on average 21.0 hours per week playing the game … and spend on average 7.7 hours per week watching TV … The national average for TV watching per week is around 28, which is what the above averages add up to. In other words, this lends support to the claim that time that was spent watching TV has been displaced by MMORPG playing" [3]. Tyler's conclusion is that "it is clear that existing studies are collectively uncertain on the question of whether the enhancement of digital play is at the same time obsolescing television" [3].

His account of why the check is hard is more useful than the result. "Accurate and detailing records of the time individuals spend with a particular medium is frequently hard to obtain, and virtually impossible after the event" [3]. Multitasking and convergence make "time spent" a poor proxy for displacement, and establishing that one medium's rise caused another's decline requires more than a correlation in hours. The obsolescence quadrant is the easiest of the four to operationalise, because it names a quantity that surveys already measure. It still comes out undecided.

The applied literature reviewed in section 2 does not supply what is missing. The smartphone tetrad concedes that "multiple interpretations are possible" and that its own readings rest on the author's perceptions [1]. Its forward-looking claim is that the tetrad "allows one to reflect the past and to try to predict – or at least speculate – about future developments" [1] — speculation, explicitly, not verification. The engineering and software-testing applications make pedagogical and practical claims for the tetrad, not predictive ones [7][8]. Searches for a formal experiment, a coding scheme with inter-coder reliability, or a prediction scored after the fact found applied tetrad papers on video conferencing, Microsoft Teams, cop-watching, generative AI and soundscape composition, but no study that treats the four laws as hypotheses to be confirmed or refuted. Only the bibliographic records of those papers were obtained, so this is a statement about what was found, not proof that nothing exists.

What the record supports, then, is a specific negative finding: no one has tested the tetrad as a set of laws. The tests that exist are fit-checks of one quadrant against survey data, and they disagree with each other. Tyler's resolution is the one the evidence best supports — "The diversity of results from the tetrad's application need not be a problem--once we dispense with pretensions to scientific uniformity--so long as these provide illuminating insights into the matter at hand" [3]. On that reading, what can be assessed is whether a tetrad analysis illuminates a case. That is a judgement about an argument, and it is graded case by case rather than by a method that would let a reader check the answer. Tyler is explicit that the tetrad is a heuristic rather than a science, while still using it [3]. No source read for this report does otherwise.


## Beyond this question

The record's other McLuhan work uses the tetrad as a probe on contemporary media — pricing algorithms, digital task managers, recommendation systems. That use is defensible on the evidence here, but only with the discipline Tyler's own applied tetrad models: each quadrant anchored in cited research, contrary evidence reported, terms defined, and scope narrowed on purpose [3]. The wine example is the warning. Two tetrads for one artefact, on one page, is what happens when the four slots are filled by fluency rather than by evidence [3].

The one place the evidence points toward something testable is Harman's reading of retrieval as the quadrant under human control [4]. If retrieval is a design decision — decontextualize an old medium, adapt it to new circumstances — then it makes predictions about what a designer will do and what will happen when they do it. Nothing in this literature has tested that. It is the most promising route from the tetrad to something falsifiable, and it requires treating the four laws as one specific claim about designers rather than as a universal grammar of artefacts.

## Open questions

One flag on section 2 should be recorded here rather than fixed. The laser-cleaning paper is described from its title and abstract only, because the full text was not obtained; the description is limited to what those state and should be read that way.

Whether the tetrad can be made falsifiable at all is unsettled, and the two most-cited critics do not address the same question. Tyler argues it cannot and should not be [3]. Harman does not discuss testability, treating the tetrad as a philosophical fourfold with a design application [4]. No source read here proposes a coding scheme, an inter-coder reliability test, or a pre-registered prediction derived from the four laws.

What "testing the tetrad" would even mean is undefined in the literature. Three different things could be tested: whether independent analysts converge on the same four answers (the McLuhans' own claim [3]); whether a quadrant's implied prediction holds in data (Tyler's check on obsolescence [3]); or whether a tetrad analysis produces insight a rival frame would miss. Only the second has been attempted, once, and it came out undecided [3]. The third has not been operationalised anywhere found.

Coverage in this report is uneven and should be read that way. Tom Tyler's article and Graham Harman's essay were read in full. Eriksen's 1996 trial was read in full. The 1976 Venable–McLuhan exchange in *Technology and Culture* was not obtained; the account of it here rests on Tyler's citation of it as the sustained critique [3]. The Lindia and Levinson material on McLuhan's Popper joke and the 1978 tetrad conference was not reached at all, so the report says nothing about Levinson's tetrad wheels or about how the McLuhan circle itself understood the falsifiability claim. Robert Logan's *Understanding New Media*, the most-cited direct extension of the tetrad to digital media, was also not read; only its bibliographic record was obtained, so the section on applications is thinner on the media-ecology mainstream than the question warrants. The 1975 *Technology and Culture* article that first stated the laws, and *The Lost Tetrads of Marshall McLuhan* (2017), were likewise not read; both are cited here only through secondary references.

The applied literature is sampled, not surveyed. Searches surfaced post-1988 tetrad papers on video conferencing, Microsoft Teams, cop-watching, generative AI and intellectual property, and soundscape composition, but only their bibliographic records were obtained. Any of them could contain the empirical test this report says is missing, and none was read. The claim that no one has tested the tetrad is a claim about what this pass found, not a proof of absence.

One source used for a passing point in section 4 — the essay in *Transforming McLuhan* that calls the four laws unverifiable — is known only through a full-text search index of the book, not from the essay itself. No stronger version of that source was obtained, and nothing in the report rests on it beyond the observation that the objection circulates in the field.

Two related questions remain open. Whether the determinism charge is answered by redefining obsolescence as remediation [3] depends on how much of a medium's effect the tetrad attributes to users rather than to the artefact, and no source read here resolves that. And the question of whether a non-falsifiable probe earns its keep — whether tetrad analyses illuminate cases that rival frames miss — has no evidence either way in this literature.
